title: PVO: Tony Burke's claim we're not a mass migration nation ignores data
text:
Published:  10:52 AEST, 18 September 2026   |  Updated:  10:54 AEST, 18 September 2026

128

View  comments

Immigration Minister Tony Burke is living in denial. He claims that it's 'absurd' to suggest Australia is a mass immigration country. What an absurd falsehood his denial is.

It's dripping with cynicism that you can lie and get away with it if you sound confident enough. It's a George Costanza moment from Seinfeld: it's not a lie if you believe it.

No wonder voters don't trust this government to tell the simple truth.

Australia has been a mass immigration country for many years. We all know that before even turning to the data that proves it.

This isn't merely a dispute about terminology, it's an exercise in national gaslighting on a grand scale.

Australians aren't stupid. The evidence against Burke's bulls*** is overwhelming.

In July 1998, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) published population projections running all the way through to 2051. Back then, Australia had 18.5 million people.

Under the ABS's lowest projection, the population would reach 23.5 million in 2051. Its highest projection (based on annual net overseas migration of 90,000 which was the norm at the time) put the population at 26.4 million come 2051.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke unveiled a sweeping overhaul of Australia's migration system in his National Press Club address on Thursday

The Australian population passed 28 million in June this year, reaching that level 25 years earlier than projected (stock image)

Where are we now? The Australian population passed 28 million in June this year. We are already 1.6 million people above the highest population the ABS thought we might reach in 2051.

We got there 25 years early, because of mass immigration. Apparently pointing this out is now 'absurd'.

It requires a special kind of contempt to look Australians in the eye and insist that white is black, up is down and the crushing pressure on housing and infrastructure is merely a figment of our collective imaginations.

World Bank data is just as devastating for Burke's false claims as the ABS data is. Between 2000 and 2025, Australia's population increased by approximately 45 per cent.

Across the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the increase was around 17 per cent. We are therefore growing at almost three times the OECD average, thanks to mass immigration.

The US grew by about 21 per cent and Britain by roughly 18 per cent. Even Canada and New Zealand, two other famously high migration countries, grew more slowly than Australia has.

Net overseas migration was still 292,000 in the year to March, equivalent to just over one per cent of Australia's entire population in a single year. It remains more than three times the 'high' annual migration assumption used by the ABS in 1998.

Words have meaning. When one of the fastest growing developed countries adds hundreds of thousands of people each and every year to its population base, calling it mass migration is hardly some wild conspiracy theory.

Australia already has 1.6 million people above the highest population the ABS thought we might reach in 2051 (stock image of metro passenger queues)

Is Minister Tony Burke is living in denial?

Burke doesn't have to like the phrase, but he can't declare the underlying reality as imaginary. When he does, his ridiculous spin needs to be called out.

His supposed knockout statistic in his National Press Club speech was his false claim that Australia's population in 2030-31 is expected to be 700,000 lower than projected before the pandemic.

That is an insult masquerading as analysis.

Australia closed its international border for two years during Covid. Of course the population temporarily fell behind a projection made before anyone imagined the border would close.

Burke is effectively arguing the post-pandemic migration surge isn't large because it has not yet completely filled the hole created by an unprecedented border shutdown.

When a convenient pre-pandemic projection makes current population growth look smaller, Burke treats it as holy writ. When Labor's own migration forecasts are comprehensively smashed to pieces, ministers quickly move on.

Do we even trust the forecast Burke leaned on to dispute the existence of mass immigration?

The October 2022 Budget forecast a net overseas migration total of 235,000 for the year 2022-23. The actual figure was 518,000. Labor missed its forecast by 283,000 people. The actual intake was more than double what it told Australians to expect.

This graph shows just how much Australia's population has grown compared to other nations

The Albanese government's immigration overhaul reflects a belief that voters will accept contested claims if they are delivered confidently, Peter van Onselen (pictured) writes

That wasn't a rounding error. It was a failure to control inflows on a scale large enough to transform demand for housing, rentals, roads, schools and health services.

Now the same government asks Australians to trust it when it says that migration will fall to 245,000 this financial year and 225,000 thereafter.

Why should we? Especially when they are defined by broken promise after broken promise. Trust is in very short supply, for good reason.

Burke's grand announcement didn't even establish a new lower target. It unveiled a collection of measures designed to meet the target Labor already had.

After repeatedly failing to deliver what it promised in the past, Labor is demanding credit for another promise made but yet to be delivered.

Some of the measures Burke outlined are sensible. Visa hopping should be curtailed. Visitor visas should not become backdoor migration pathways. Students should not be able to move endlessly between dubious courses simply to prolong their stay. Overstayers should be required to leave.

But the need for those changes proves that the system has not been under control. Labor has been in office for more than four years already, so whose fault is that?

Burke wants credit for closing loopholes Labor allowed to remain open while simultaneously ridiculing anyone who noticed the consequences.

The changes will slash access to extended working holiday visas and make it harder for temporary migrants to remain in the country by repeatedly switching visas

The Immigration Minister also insists migration is not primarily responsible for the housing crisis, pointing instead to declining household sizes. Fewer people living in each dwelling has certainly added to demand.

But it does not erase the effect of adding hundreds of thousands of people every year to the national population total.

Noting, of course, that Burke reckons doing so isn't mass immigration.

Net overseas migration accounted for almost three-quarters of Australia's population growth in the latest ABS figures. Every additional person needs somewhere to live. That is not xenophobia, it's not dog whistling. It is basic arithmetic.

Indeed, Burke's own policy acknowledges this relationship. He says reducing migration demand while prioritising construction workers will help housing.

He can't simultaneously boast that lower migration will ease housing pressure and dismiss the suggestion that high migration intensified it. Nor is this necessarily an argument against immigration.

Australia is a migrant nation and has benefited enormously from skilled arrivals. The argument is about scale, composition and whether population growth is matched by housing and infrastructure.

Reasonable people can disagree about the right number. What they should not tolerate is a minister declaring the debate illegitimate because the facts are politically inconvenient to him.

Burke could have admitted that Labor allowed migration to surge beyond the country's capacity to absorb it. He could have explained why the forecasts were so badly wrong, accepted the consequences and made the case for the government's preferred future intake.

Instead, he told Australians that describing what happened as 'mass migration' was absurd.

Trust is not simply about whether every government forecast proves accurate.

Forecasts inevitably change. Trust depends on whether ministers admit mistakes, acknowledge obvious facts and speak honestly when reality becomes politically uncomfortable.

Labor has done none of these things.

It lost control of migration, missed its own forecasts by hundreds of thousands, allowed population growth to outrun housing supply and then waited until One Nation surged in the polls before unveiling its supposed crackdown.

Now it wants Australians to believe this was always the plan, and that anyone who describes the scale of migration in plain English is the unreasonable one.

It's cowardice dressed up as an alternative reality.

The absurdity is not the claim that Australia has experienced mass migration. It is Tony Burke expecting Australians to trust a government that first lost control of the numbers and is now trying to deny what those numbers mean.
